Conditional statements: A conditional statement has the form if p, then q. The if part is the hypothesis and the then part is the conclusion. The converse switches them (if q, then p), the inverse negates both (if not p, then not q) and the contrapositive switches and negates (if not q, then not p). A conditional and its contrapositive always have the same truth value. A conditional is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false, and one example like that is a counterexample. If a conditional and its converse are both true, they combine into a biconditional using if and only if.
Deductive reasoning: Inductive reasoning finds a pattern from examples and makes a conjecture, which can be wrong. Deductive reasoning uses facts, definitions and rules to reach a conclusion that must be true. The Law of Detachment says that if p implies q is true and p is true, then q is true. The Law of Syllogism says that if p implies q and q implies r are true, then p implies r is true. A conjecture is disproved by a single counterexample.
Angles and parallel lines: A transversal is a line that crosses two or more other lines. When the lines are parallel: corresponding angles are congruent, alternate interior angles are congruent, alternate exterior angles are congruent and consecutive (same-side) interior angles are supplementary. Vertical angles are always congruent and a linear pair is always supplementary. The converses are also true, so if corresponding angles or alternate interior angles are congruent, or consecutive interior angles are supplementary, the lines are parallel.
Writing two-column proofs: A proof is a logical argument that shows a statement is true. A two-column proof lists statements in the left column and the reason for each statement in the right column. It begins with the given information and ends with what you want to prove. Reasons can be given facts, definitions, postulates, properties of equality (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, substitution, distributive) and theorems that were already proved. Every statement must have a reason, and you cannot use what you are trying to prove.
